# Hackachusetts_CodeTutor
=======
# Monaco Editor

[![Versions](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/monaco-editor)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/monaco-editor)
[![Versions](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/monaco-editor/next)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/monaco-editor)
[![Feature Requests](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/microsoft/monaco-editor/feature-request.svg)](https://github.com/microsoft/monaco-editor/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3Afeature-request+sort%3Areactions-%2B1-desc)
[![Bugs](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/microsoft/monaco-editor/bug.svg)](https://github.com/microsoft/monaco-editor/issues?utf8=✓&q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3Abug)

The Monaco Editor is the fully featured code editor from [VS Code](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode). Check out the [VS Code docs](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/editingevolved) to see some of the supported features.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5047891/94183711-290c0780-fea3-11ea-90e3-c88ff9d21bd6.png)

## Try it out

Try out the editor and see various examples [in our interactive playground](https://microsoft.github.io/monaco-editor/playground.html).

The playground is the best way to learn about how to use the editor, which features is supports, to try out different versions and to create minimal reproducible examples for bug reports.

## Installing

```
> npm install monaco-editor
```

You will get:

- inside `/esm`: ESM version of the editor (compatible with e.g. webpack)
- `monaco.d.ts`: this specifies the API of the editor (this is what is actually versioned, everything else is considered private and might break with any release).

:warning: The monaco editor also ships an `AMD` build for backwards-compatibility reasons, but the `AMD` support is deprecated and will be removed in future versions.

## Localization

To load the editor in a specific language, make sure that the corresponding nls script file is loaded before the main monaco editor script. For example, to load the editor in German, include the following script tag:
```html
<script src="path/to/monaco-editor/esm/nls.messages.de.js"></script>
```

Check the sources for available languages.

## Concepts

Monaco editor is best known for being the text editor that powers VS Code. However, it's a bit more nuanced. Some basic understanding about the underlying concepts is needed to use Monaco editor effectively.

### Models

Models are at the heart of Monaco editor. It's what you interact with when managing content. A model represents a file that has been opened. This could represent a file that exists on a file system, but it doesn't have to. For example, the model holds the text content, determines the language of the content, and tracks the edit history of the content.

### URIs

Each model is identified by a URI. This is why it's not possible for two models to have the same URI. Ideally when you represent content in Monaco editor, you should think of a virtual file system that matches the files your users are editing. For example, you could use `file:///` as a base path. If a model is created without a URI, its URI will be `inmemory://model/1`. The number increases as more models are created.

### Editors

An editor is a user facing view of the model. This is what gets attached to the DOM and what your users see visually. Typical editor operations are displaying a model, managing the view state, or executing actions or commands.

### Providers

Providers provide smart editor features. For example, this includes completion and hover information. It is not the same as, but often maps to [language server protocol](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol) features.

Providers work on models. Some smart features depends on the file URI. For example, for TypeScript to resolve imports, or for JSON IntelliSense to determine which JSON schema to apply to which model. So it's important to choose proper model URIs.

### Disposables

Many Monaco related objects often implement the `.dispose()` method. This method is intended to perform cleanups when a resource is no longer needed. For example, calling `model.dispose()` will unregister it, freeing up the URI for a new model. Editors should be disposed to free up resources and remove their model listeners.

## Documentation

- Learn how to integrate the editor with these [complete samples](./samples/).
  - [Integrate the ESM version](./docs/integrate-esm.md)
- Learn how to use the editor API and try out your own customizations in the [playground](https://microsoft.github.io/monaco-editor/playground.html).
- Explore the [API docs](https://microsoft.github.io/monaco-editor/docs.html) or read them straight from [`monaco.d.ts`](https://github.com/microsoft/monaco-editor/blob/gh-pages/node_modules/monaco-editor/monaco.d.ts).
- Read [this guide](https://github.com/microsoft/monaco-editor/wiki/Accessibility-Guide-for-Integrators) to ensure the editor is accessible to all your users!
- Create a Monarch tokenizer for a new programming language [in the Monarch playground](https://microsoft.github.io/monaco-editor/monarch.html).
- Ask questions on [StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/monaco-editor)! Search open and closed issues, there are a lot of tips in there!

## Issues

Create [issues](https://github.com/microsoft/monaco-editor/issues) in this repository for anything related to the Monaco Editor. Please search for existing issues to avoid duplicates.

## FAQ

❓ **What is the relationship between VS Code and the Monaco Editor?**

The Monaco Editor is generated straight from VS Code's sources with some shims around services the code needs to make it run in a web browser outside of its home.

❓ **What is the relationship between VS Code's version and the Monaco Editor's version?**

None. The Monaco Editor is a library and it reflects directly the source code.

❓ **I've written an extension for VS Code, will it work on the Monaco Editor in a browser?**

No.

> Note: If the extension is fully based on the [LSP](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/) and if the language server is authored in JavaScript, then it would be possible.

❓ **Why all these web workers and why should I care?**

Language services create web workers to compute heavy stuff outside of the UI thread. They cost hardly anything in terms of resource overhead and you shouldn't worry too much about them, as long as you get them to work (see above the cross-domain case).

❓ **I see the warning "Could not create web worker". What should I do?**

HTML5 does not allow pages loaded on `file://` to create web workers. Please load the editor with a web server on `http://` or `https://` schemes.

❓ **Is the editor supported in mobile browsers or mobile web app frameworks?**

No.

❓ **Why doesn't the editor support TextMate grammars?**

- Please see https://github.com/bolinfest/monaco-tm which puts together `monaco-editor`, `vscode-oniguruma` and `vscode-textmate` to get TM grammar support in the editor.

**Scope of C support.** Writing a full C compiler/interpreter is out of scope for a hackathon. **When you hit Play:**
- `togglePlay` sets `playing = true`. If you were parked on the last state, it first jumps back to state 0 so Play replays from the top.

import { useCallback, useEffect, useRef, useState } from "react";
import type { ExecutionTrace } from "./trace";

export interface Stepper {
  /** Current step index (clamped to the trace). */
  step: number;
  /** Total number of states. */
  total: number;
  /** True while auto-play is running. */
  playing: boolean;
  /** Delay between auto-play steps, in ms. */
  speedMs: number;

  atStart: boolean;
  atEnd: boolean;

  /** Jump to an arbitrary step (used by the slider). */
  goTo: (step: number) => void;
  /** Step into: advance exactly one execution step (descends into calls). */
  stepInto: () => void;
  /** Step over: run any call on this line to completion, stop at same depth. */
  stepOver: () => void;
  /** Step out: run until we return to a shallower call-stack depth. */
  stepOut: () => void;
  /** Step back one state. */
  stepBack: () => void;
  /** Restart at the first state. */
  restart: () => void;
  /** Toggle auto-play. */
  togglePlay: () => void;
  setSpeedMs: (ms: number) => void;
}

/**
 * Owns playback position over an execution trace and implements the debugger
 * stepping semantics using each state's `depth`:
 *   - step into = next index
 *   - step over = next index whose depth <= current depth
 *   - step out  = next index whose depth <  current depth
 * Depth is optional in the trace; when absent, over/out behave like into.
 */
export function useStepper(trace: ExecutionTrace): Stepper {
  const states = trace.states;
  const total = states.length;

  const [step, setStep] = useState(0);
  const [playing, setPlaying] = useState(false);
  // Default to 1x (1.5s per state) so learners can follow each change.
  const [speedMs, setSpeedMs] = useState(1500);

  // Keep step in range if the trace shrinks (e.g. a new run).
  const clamped = Math.min(step, Math.max(0, total - 1));
  const atStart = clamped <= 0;
  const atEnd = clamped >= total - 1;

  const depthAt = useCallback(
    (i: number) => states[i]?.depth ?? 1,
    [states]
  );

  const goTo = useCallback(
    (next: number) => {
      setStep(Math.min(Math.max(0, next), Math.max(0, total - 1)));
    },
    [total]
  );

  const stepInto = useCallback(() => {
    setStep((s) => Math.min(s + 1, total - 1));
  }, [total]);

  const stepBack = useCallback(() => {
    setStep((s) => Math.max(s - 1, 0));
  }, []);

  const stepOver = useCallback(() => {
    setStep((s) => {
      const curDepth = depthAt(s);
      for (let i = s + 1; i < total; i++) {
        if (depthAt(i) <= curDepth) return i;
      }
      return total - 1;
    });
  }, [depthAt, total]);

  const stepOut = useCallback(() => {
    setStep((s) => {
      const curDepth = depthAt(s);
      for (let i = s + 1; i < total; i++) {
        if (depthAt(i) < curDepth) return i;
      }
      return total - 1;
    });
  }, [depthAt, total]);

  const restart = useCallback(() => {
    setPlaying(false);
    setStep(0);
  }, []);

  const togglePlay = useCallback(() => {
    setPlaying((p) => {
      // If starting playback from the end, restart from the top.
      if (!p && step >= total - 1) setStep(0);
      return !p;
    });
  }, [step, total]);

  // Auto-play timer: advance one step each tick; stop at the end.
  const playingRef = useRef(playing);
  playingRef.current = playing;
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!playing) return;
    if (clamped >= total - 1) {
      setPlaying(false);
      return;
    }
    const id = window.setTimeout(() => {
      setStep((s) => {
        const next = Math.min(s + 1, total - 1);
        if (next >= total - 1) setPlaying(false);
        return next;
      });
    }, speedMs);
    return () => window.clearTimeout(id);
  }, [playing, clamped, total, speedMs]);

  return {
    step: clamped,
    total,
    playing,
    speedMs,
    atStart,
    atEnd,
    goTo,
    stepInto,
    stepOver,
    stepOut,
    stepBack,
    restart,
    togglePlay,
    setSpeedMs,
  };
}

//! C language support: lex -> parse -> interpret -> ExecutionTrace.

pub mod ast;
pub mod interp;
pub mod lexer;
pub mod parser;

use crate::trace::ExecutionTrace;

/// A user-facing error from running C code, with an optional source line.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct CError {
    /// "lex" | "parse" | "runtime".
    pub stage: &'static str,
    pub message: String,
    pub line: Option<usize>,
}

/// Lex, parse, and interpret a C program, producing an execution trace.
pub fn run(source: &str) -> Result<ExecutionTrace, CError> {
    let tokens = lexer::lex(source).map_err(|e| CError {
        stage: "lex",
        message: e.message,
        line: Some(e.line),
    })?;

    let mut parser = parser::Parser::new(tokens);
    let program = parser.parse_program().map_err(|e| CError {
        stage: "parse",
        message: e.message,
        line: Some(e.line),
    })?;

    let interp = interp::Interp::new(&program);
    interp.run().map_err(|e| CError {
        stage: "runtime",
        message: e.message,
        line: if e.line == 0 { None } else { Some(e.line) },
    })
}

//! AST for the supported subset of C.

/// A declared/base type. Pointers are tracked by `pointer_depth`.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
pub enum BaseType {
    Int,
    Char,
    Double,
    Float,
    Long,
    Void,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
pub struct CType {
    pub base: BaseType,
    /// Number of `*` levels (0 = plain value, 1 = `int*`, etc.).
    pub pointer_depth: u32,
}

impl CType {
    pub fn display(&self) -> String {
        let base = match self.base {
            BaseType::Int => "int",
            BaseType::Char => "char",
            BaseType::Double => "double",
            BaseType::Float => "float",
            BaseType::Long => "long",
            BaseType::Void => "void",
        };
        format!("{}{}", base, "*".repeat(self.pointer_depth as usize))
    }
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
pub enum BinOp {
    Add,
    Sub,
    Mul,
    Div,
    Mod,
    Eq,
    Ne,
    Lt,
    Gt,
    Le,
    Ge,
    And,
    Or,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
pub enum UnOp {
    Neg,
    Not,
    /// Address-of: &x
    AddrOf,
    /// Dereference: *p
    Deref,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub enum Expr {
    IntLit(i64),
    FloatLit(f64),
    CharLit(char),
    StrLit(String),
    Ident(String),
    /// Array indexing: base[index]
    Index(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>),
    /// Unary operation.
    Unary(UnOp, Box<Expr>),
    /// Binary operation.
    Binary(BinOp, Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>),
    /// Assignment: target = value. Target is an lvalue expression.
    Assign(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>),
    /// Function call: name(args...).
    Call(String, Vec<Expr>),
    /// Pre/post increment/decrement; bool = is_prefix, i64 = +1/-1.
    IncDec { target: Box<Expr>, delta: i64, prefix: bool },
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub enum Stmt {
    /// Variable declaration, optionally with an initializer.
    /// For arrays, `array_len` is Some(n).
    VarDecl {
        ty: CType,
        name: String,
        array_len: Option<usize>,
        init: Option<Expr>,
        /// For `int a[] = {1,2,3}` or `int a[3] = {...}`.
        array_init: Option<Vec<Expr>>,
        line: usize,
    },
    ExprStmt(Expr, usize),
    If {
        cond: Expr,
        then_branch: Vec<Stmt>,
        else_branch: Option<Vec<Stmt>>,
        line: usize,
    },
    While {
        cond: Expr,
        body: Vec<Stmt>,
        line: usize,
    },
    For {
        init: Option<Box<Stmt>>,
        cond: Option<Expr>,
        step: Option<Expr>,
        body: Vec<Stmt>,
        line: usize,
    },
    Return(Option<Expr>, usize),
    Break(usize),
    Continue(usize),
    Block(Vec<Stmt>),
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct Param {
    pub ty: CType,
    pub name: String,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct Function {
    /// Return type (kept for future type checking / coercion of return values).
    #[allow(dead_code)]
    pub ret: CType,
    pub name: String,
    pub params: Vec<Param>,
    pub body: Vec<Stmt>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct Program {
    pub functions: Vec<Function>,
}

//! Recursive-descent parser for the supported subset of C.

use super::ast::*;
use super::lexer::{Tok, Token};

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct ParseError {
    pub message: String,
    pub line: usize,
}

pub struct Parser {
    toks: Vec<Token>,
    pos: usize,
}

type PResult<T> = Result<T, ParseError>;

impl Parser {
    pub fn new(toks: Vec<Token>) -> Self {
        Parser { toks, pos: 0 }
    }

    pub fn parse_program(&mut self) -> PResult<Program> {
        let mut functions = Vec::new();
        while !self.check(&Tok::Eof) {
            functions.push(self.parse_function()?);
        }
        Ok(Program { functions })
    }

    // ---- token helpers ----------------------------------------------------

    fn peek(&self) -> &Tok {
        &self.toks[self.pos].tok
    }

    fn peek_at(&self, offset: usize) -> &Tok {
        let idx = (self.pos + offset).min(self.toks.len() - 1);
        &self.toks[idx].tok
    }

    fn line(&self) -> usize {
        self.toks[self.pos].line
    }

    fn check(&self, t: &Tok) -> bool {
        self.peek() == t
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) -> Tok {
        let t = self.toks[self.pos].tok.clone();
        if self.pos < self.toks.len() - 1 {
            self.pos += 1;
        }
        t
    }

    fn eat(&mut self, t: &Tok) -> PResult<()> {
        if self.check(t) {
            self.advance();
            Ok(())
        } else {
            Err(ParseError {
                message: format!("expected {:?}, found {:?}", t, self.peek()),
                line: self.line(),
            })
        }
    }

    fn match_tok(&mut self, t: &Tok) -> bool {
        if self.check(t) {
            self.advance();
            true
        } else {
            false
        }
    }

    // ---- types ------------------------------------------------------------

    fn is_type_start(&self) -> bool {
        matches!(
            self.peek(),
            Tok::KwInt
                | Tok::KwChar
                | Tok::KwDouble
                | Tok::KwFloat
                | Tok::KwVoid
                | Tok::KwLong
        )
    }

    fn parse_type(&mut self) -> PResult<CType> {
        let base = match self.advance() {
            Tok::KwInt => BaseType::Int,
            Tok::KwChar => BaseType::Char,
            Tok::KwDouble => BaseType::Double,
            Tok::KwFloat => BaseType::Float,
            Tok::KwLong => BaseType::Long,
            Tok::KwVoid => BaseType::Void,
            other => {
                return Err(ParseError {
                    message: format!("expected a type, found {:?}", other),
                    line: self.line(),
                })
            }
        };
        let mut pointer_depth = 0;
        while self.match_tok(&Tok::Star) {
            pointer_depth += 1;
        }
        Ok(CType { base, pointer_depth })
    }

    fn expect_ident(&mut self) -> PResult<String> {
        match self.advance() {
            Tok::Ident(name) => Ok(name),
            other => Err(ParseError {
                message: format!("expected identifier, found {:?}", other),
                line: self.line(),
            }),
        }
    }

    // ---- functions --------------------------------------------------------

    fn parse_function(&mut self) -> PResult<Function> {
        let ret = self.parse_type()?;
        let name = self.expect_ident()?;
        self.eat(&Tok::LParen)?;
        let mut params = Vec::new();
        if !self.check(&Tok::RParen) {
            // Handle `void` param list.
            if self.check(&Tok::KwVoid) && self.peek_at(1) == &Tok::RParen {
                self.advance();
            } else {
                loop {
                    let ty = self.parse_type()?;
                    let pname = self.expect_ident()?;
                    params.push(Param { ty, name: pname });
                    if !self.match_tok(&Tok::Comma) {
                        break;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        self.eat(&Tok::RParen)?;
        self.eat(&Tok::LBrace)?;
        let body = self.parse_block_body()?;
        Ok(Function { ret, name, params, body })
    }

    /// Parse statements until a closing brace (which is consumed).
    fn parse_block_body(&mut self) -> PResult<Vec<Stmt>> {
        let mut stmts = Vec::new();
        while !self.check(&Tok::RBrace) && !self.check(&Tok::Eof) {
            stmts.push(self.parse_stmt()?);
        }
        self.eat(&Tok::RBrace)?;
        Ok(stmts)
    }

    // ---- statements -------------------------------------------------------

    fn parse_stmt(&mut self) -> PResult<Stmt> {
        let line = self.line();
        match self.peek() {
            Tok::LBrace => {
                self.advance();
                Ok(Stmt::Block(self.parse_block_body()?))
            }
            Tok::KwIf => self.parse_if(),
            Tok::KwWhile => self.parse_while(),
            Tok::KwFor => self.parse_for(),
            Tok::KwReturn => {
                self.advance();
                let expr = if self.check(&Tok::Semicolon) {
                    None
                } else {
                    Some(self.parse_expr()?)
                };
                self.eat(&Tok::Semicolon)?;
                Ok(Stmt::Return(expr, line))
            }
            Tok::KwBreak => {
                self.advance();
                self.eat(&Tok::Semicolon)?;
                Ok(Stmt::Break(line))
            }
            Tok::KwContinue => {
                self.advance();
                self.eat(&Tok::Semicolon)?;
                Ok(Stmt::Continue(line))
            }
            _ if self.is_type_start() => self.parse_var_decl(),
            _ => {
                let expr = self.parse_expr()?;
                self.eat(&Tok::Semicolon)?;
                Ok(Stmt::ExprStmt(expr, line))
            }
        }
    }

    fn parse_var_decl(&mut self) -> PResult<Stmt> {
        let line = self.line();
        let ty = self.parse_type()?;
        let name = self.expect_ident()?;

        // Array declaration: name[len]
        let mut array_len = None;
        if self.match_tok(&Tok::LBracket) {
            if let Tok::Int(n) = self.peek().clone() {
                self.advance();
                array_len = Some(n as usize);
            } else {
                array_len = Some(0); // size inferred from initializer
            }
            self.eat(&Tok::RBracket)?;
        }

        let mut init = None;
        let mut array_init = None;
        if self.match_tok(&Tok::Assign) {
            if self.check(&Tok::LBrace) {
                // Array initializer list { a, b, c }
                self.advance();
                let mut elems = Vec::new();
                if !self.check(&Tok::RBrace) {
                    loop {
                        elems.push(self.parse_expr()?);
                        if !self.match_tok(&Tok::Comma) {
                            break;
                        }
                        if self.check(&Tok::RBrace) {
                            break;
                        }
                    }
                }
                self.eat(&Tok::RBrace)?;
                if array_len.is_none() {
                    array_len = Some(elems.len());
                }
                array_init = Some(elems);
            } else {
                init = Some(self.parse_expr()?);
            }
        }
        self.eat(&Tok::Semicolon)?;
        Ok(Stmt::VarDecl {
            ty,
            name,
            array_len,
            init,
            array_init,
            line,
        })
    }

    fn parse_if(&mut self) -> PResult<Stmt> {
        let line = self.line();
        self.eat(&Tok::KwIf)?;
        self.eat(&Tok::LParen)?;
        let cond = self.parse_expr()?;
        self.eat(&Tok::RParen)?;
        let then_branch = self.parse_stmt_as_block()?;
        let else_branch = if self.match_tok(&Tok::KwElse) {
            Some(self.parse_stmt_as_block()?)
        } else {
            None
        };
        Ok(Stmt::If { cond, then_branch, else_branch, line })
    }

    fn parse_while(&mut self) -> PResult<Stmt> {
        let line = self.line();
        self.eat(&Tok::KwWhile)?;
        self.eat(&Tok::LParen)?;
        let cond = self.parse_expr()?;
        self.eat(&Tok::RParen)?;
        let body = self.parse_stmt_as_block()?;
        Ok(Stmt::While { cond, body, line })
    }

    fn parse_for(&mut self) -> PResult<Stmt> {
        let line = self.line();
        self.eat(&Tok::KwFor)?;
        self.eat(&Tok::LParen)?;

        let init = if self.check(&Tok::Semicolon) {
            self.advance();
            None
        } else if self.is_type_start() {
            Some(Box::new(self.parse_var_decl()?))
        } else {
            let e = self.parse_expr()?;
            self.eat(&Tok::Semicolon)?;
            Some(Box::new(Stmt::ExprStmt(e, line)))
        };

        let cond = if self.check(&Tok::Semicolon) {
            None
        } else {
            Some(self.parse_expr()?)
        };
        self.eat(&Tok::Semicolon)?;

        let step = if self.check(&Tok::RParen) {
            None
        } else {
            Some(self.parse_expr()?)
        };
        self.eat(&Tok::RParen)?;

        let body = self.parse_stmt_as_block()?;
        Ok(Stmt::For { init, cond, step, body, line })
    }

    /// Parse a single statement, wrapping a non-block as a one-element block.
    fn parse_stmt_as_block(&mut self) -> PResult<Vec<Stmt>> {
        if self.check(&Tok::LBrace) {
            self.advance();
            self.parse_block_body()
        } else {
            Ok(vec![self.parse_stmt()?])
        }
    }

    // ---- expressions (precedence climbing) --------------------------------

    fn parse_expr(&mut self) -> PResult<Expr> {
        self.parse_assignment()
    }

    fn parse_assignment(&mut self) -> PResult<Expr> {
        let left = self.parse_logic_or()?;
        match self.peek() {
            Tok::Assign => {
                self.advance();
                let right = self.parse_assignment()?;
                Ok(Expr::Assign(Box::new(left), Box::new(right)))
            }
            Tok::PlusEq | Tok::MinusEq | Tok::StarEq | Tok::SlashEq => {
                let op = match self.advance() {
                    Tok::PlusEq => BinOp::Add,
                    Tok::MinusEq => BinOp::Sub,
                    Tok::StarEq => BinOp::Mul,
                    Tok::SlashEq => BinOp::Div,
                    _ => unreachable!(),
                };
                let right = self.parse_assignment()?;
                // a += b  =>  a = a + b
                let combined = Expr::Binary(op, Box::new(left.clone()), Box::new(right));
                Ok(Expr::Assign(Box::new(left), Box::new(combined)))
            }
            _ => Ok(left),
        }
    }

    fn parse_logic_or(&mut self) -> PResult<Expr> {
        let mut left = self.parse_logic_and()?;
        while self.check(&Tok::OrOr) {
            self.advance();
            let right = self.parse_logic_and()?;
            left = Expr::Binary(BinOp::Or, Box::new(left), Box::new(right));
        }
        Ok(left)
    }

    fn parse_logic_and(&mut self) -> PResult<Expr> {
        let mut left = self.parse_equality()?;
        while self.check(&Tok::AndAnd) {
            self.advance();
            let right = self.parse_equality()?;
            left = Expr::Binary(BinOp::And, Box::new(left), Box::new(right));
        }
        Ok(left)
    }

    fn parse_equality(&mut self) -> PResult<Expr> {
        let mut left = self.parse_relational()?;
        loop {
            let op = match self.peek() {
                Tok::Eq => BinOp::Eq,
                Tok::Ne => BinOp::Ne,
                _ => break,
            };
            self.advance();
            let right = self.parse_relational()?;
            left = Expr::Binary(op, Box::new(left), Box::new(right));
        }
        Ok(left)
    }

    fn parse_relational(&mut self) -> PResult<Expr> {
        let mut left = self.parse_additive()?;
        loop {
            let op = match self.peek() {
                Tok::Lt => BinOp::Lt,
                Tok::Gt => BinOp::Gt,
                Tok::Le => BinOp::Le,
                Tok::Ge => BinOp::Ge,
                _ => break,
            };
            self.advance();
            let right = self.parse_additive()?;
            left = Expr::Binary(op, Box::new(left), Box::new(right));
        }
        Ok(left)
    }

    fn parse_additive(&mut self) -> PResult<Expr> {
        let mut left = self.parse_multiplicative()?;
        loop {
            let op = match self.peek() {
                Tok::Plus => BinOp::Add,
                Tok::Minus => BinOp::Sub,
                _ => break,
            };
            self.advance();
            let right = self.parse_multiplicative()?;
            left = Expr::Binary(op, Box::new(left), Box::new(right));
        }
        Ok(left)
    }

    fn parse_multiplicative(&mut self) -> PResult<Expr> {
        let mut left = self.parse_unary()?;
        loop {
            let op = match self.peek() {
                Tok::Star => BinOp::Mul,
                Tok::Slash => BinOp::Div,
                Tok::Percent => BinOp::Mod,
                _ => break,
            };
            self.advance();
            let right = self.parse_unary()?;
            left = Expr::Binary(op, Box::new(left), Box::new(right));
        }
        Ok(left)
    }

    fn parse_unary(&mut self) -> PResult<Expr> {
        match self.peek() {
            Tok::Minus => {
                self.advance();
                Ok(Expr::Unary(UnOp::Neg, Box::new(self.parse_unary()?)))
            }
            Tok::Not => {
                self.advance();
                Ok(Expr::Unary(UnOp::Not, Box::new(self.parse_unary()?)))
            }
            Tok::Amp => {
                self.advance();
                Ok(Expr::Unary(UnOp::AddrOf, Box::new(self.parse_unary()?)))
            }
            Tok::Star => {
                self.advance();
                Ok(Expr::Unary(UnOp::Deref, Box::new(self.parse_unary()?)))
            }
            Tok::PlusPlus => {
                self.advance();
                let e = self.parse_unary()?;
                Ok(Expr::IncDec { target: Box::new(e), delta: 1, prefix: true })
            }
            Tok::MinusMinus => {
                self.advance();
                let e = self.parse_unary()?;
                Ok(Expr::IncDec { target: Box::new(e), delta: -1, prefix: true })
            }
            _ => self.parse_postfix(),
        }
    }

    fn parse_postfix(&mut self) -> PResult<Expr> {
        let mut expr = self.parse_primary()?;
        loop {
            match self.peek() {
                Tok::LBracket => {
                    self.advance();
                    let idx = self.parse_expr()?;
                    self.eat(&Tok::RBracket)?;
                    expr = Expr::Index(Box::new(expr), Box::new(idx));
                }
                Tok::PlusPlus => {
                    self.advance();
                    expr = Expr::IncDec { target: Box::new(expr), delta: 1, prefix: false };
                }
                Tok::MinusMinus => {
                    self.advance();
                    expr = Expr::IncDec { target: Box::new(expr), delta: -1, prefix: false };
                }
                _ => break,
            }
        }
        Ok(expr)
    }

    fn parse_primary(&mut self) -> PResult<Expr> {
        match self.peek().clone() {
            Tok::Int(n) => {
                self.advance();
                Ok(Expr::IntLit(n))
            }
            Tok::Float(f) => {
                self.advance();
                Ok(Expr::FloatLit(f))
            }
            Tok::Char(c) => {
                self.advance();
                Ok(Expr::CharLit(c))
            }
            Tok::Str(s) => {
                self.advance();
                Ok(Expr::StrLit(s))
            }
            Tok::LParen => {
                self.advance();
                let e = self.parse_expr()?;
                self.eat(&Tok::RParen)?;
                Ok(e)
            }
            Tok::Ident(name) => {
                self.advance();
                if self.check(&Tok::LParen) {

Great instinct — you've landed on exactly the right question, and your intuition is correct. The key realization is: **a heap of structs-with-pointers is fundamentally a directed graph, not a tree.** A tree is just the common, well-behaved case. Floyd's cycle detection, a buggy tree where two nodes point at the same child, a doubly-linked list — these are all graphs that aren't trees. So the robust approach is to lay out a *graph* but make it *look* tree-like when it happens to be one.

Here are the real options, roughly from simplest to most powerful:

**Option A — Layered (BFS) layout. This is what you're describing, and I think it's the right choice.**
Do a breadth-first traversal from the "roots" (heap objects pointed to by stack variables, e.g. `root`, `head`). Assign each node a **depth level** = its BFS distance from a root. Nodes at the same level sit in a horizontal row; a node is placed below and spread out under the node that first reached it. This gives you:
- A real tree for trees (your BST renders as a proper tree — siblings next to each other below the parent, exactly as you said).
- A clean top-to-bottom chain for a linked list.
- For a **cycle** (Floyd's): the nodes lay out in their BFS order, and the "back-edge" pointer that creates the cycle is just drawn as an arrow going back to an earlier node. So a cycle literally looks like a chain of nodes with one arrow curving back — which is exactly the mental model you want students to see. Your phrasing — "cycles shown with arrows pointing to the next pointer of a node" — is precisely this.
- A node reachable by two parents (shared child, or a diamond) gets placed once at its level, and both parents draw arrows to it. No duplication, no hiding.

The only thing BFS layout doesn't do perfectly is guarantee zero arrow crossings in dense graphs — but for the structures students actually build (trees, lists, cycles, small graphs), it reads clearly.

**Option B — Strict recursive tree layout** (position by subtree width). Prettier for *pure* trees, but it breaks the moment there's a cycle or a shared node, because "subtree width" is undefined when a node has two parents or a back-edge. I'd rule this out for exactly the reason you flagged.

**Option C — Force-directed / physics layout** (nodes repel, edges act like springs). Handles arbitrary graphs, but the layout is non-deterministic and jiggly, nodes drift around between steps, and it's much harder to follow when you're stepping through execution. Wrong fit for a tutor where you want stable, predictable positions as state changes. Rule out.

**My recommendation: Option A (layered BFS).** It gives you the proper tree for trees, a clean list for lists, and — critically — it represents cycles and tangles honestly as back-arrows rather than hiding anything or faking a tree. **1. Browser storage (localStorage) — "within the browser."**

- Con: it's tied to *that browser on that device*. Clear browser data and it's gone; switch to another computer and it's not there. No backend needed.

**2. Real device files — download/upload.**
A "Save" button downloads a `.c` file to the user's Downloads folder, and an "Open" button lets them pick a file to load back in.
- Pro: real portable files they own, can share or keep anywhere.
- Con: manual — they have to click save and pick where, and loading means re-selecting the file. Doesn't automatically survive a refresh unless combined with option 1.

**3. Server-side accounts — save to a database.**
Code stored on your Rust backend per user account, accessible from any device.
- Pro: true cross-device sync.
- Con: needs auth, user accounts, a database, backend endpoints — a large feature, overkill for a hackathon.

- **localStorage autosave** as the always-on safety net — the editor content (and language) saves continuously, so a refresh or accidental close never loses work. This directly fixes the bug you hit. This is the "within the browser" piece.

:root {
  --bg: #1e1e1e;
  --panel-bg: #252526;
  --border: #333;
  --text: #e4e4e4;
  --muted: #9a9a9a;
  --accent: #0e8adb;
  color-scheme: dark;
}

* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

html,
body,
#root {
  height: 100%;
  margin: 0;
}

body {
  background: var(--bg);
  color: var(--text);
  font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif;
}

.app {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  height: 100vh;
}

.app__header {
  padding: 0.6rem 1rem;
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border);
  display: flex;
  align-items: baseline;
  gap: 1rem;
}

/* Panel show/hide toggles, pinned to the right of the header. */
.app__toggles {
  margin-left: auto;
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 0.4rem;
}

.app__toggle {
  background: var(--panel-bg);
  color: var(--muted);
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  border-radius: 4px;
  padding: 0.25rem 0.7rem;
  font-size: 0.8rem;
  cursor: pointer;
}

.app__toggle:hover {
  border-color: var(--accent);
}

.app__toggle--on {
  color: #fff;
  background: var(--accent);
  border-color: var(--accent);
}

.app__brand {
  margin: 0;
  font-size: 1.1rem;
  letter-spacing: 0.02em;
}

.app__tagline {
  margin: 0;
  color: var(--muted);
  font-size: 0.85rem;
}

.app__main {
  flex: 1;
  min-height: 0;
}

/* Editor left, analysis right, with draggable splitters between panes. Flex
   lets panes grow/shrink via flex-basis set from the splitter drag state. */
.workspace {
  display: flex;
  height: 100%;
  min-height: 0;
}

.workspace__left {
  min-width: 0;
  min-height: 0;
  flex: 0 1 50%;
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
}

/* Thin draggable divider between two panes. */
.splitter {
  flex: 0 0 5px;
  cursor: col-resize;
  background: var(--border);
  align-self: stretch;
}

.splitter:hover {

// Horizontal layered (BFS) layout for heap objects.
//
// The heap is a directed graph: objects (structs/arrays) with pointer fields
// that reference other objects. We lay it out left-to-right:
//   - depth (distance from a root) -> column (x), increasing rightward
//   - siblings within a depth       -> stacked vertically (y)
// Roots are heap objects pointed to by stack variables; unreachable objects
// (e.g. leaked mallocs) are laid out as their own trees after the reachable
// ones so nothing is hidden.
//
// This renders trees as trees (root left, children fanning right), linked
// lists as left-to-right chains, and cycles/graphs honestly: a back-edge is
// just an arrow returning to an earlier node. It never duplicates or drops a
// node — a shared child is placed once and both parents point at it.

import {
  type ProgramState,
  type HeapObject,
  isArray,
  isStruct,
  isRef,
} from "./trace";

export interface NodeLayout {
  id: string;
  /** Top-left position within the layout canvas, in px. */
  x: number;
  y: number;
  depth: number;
}

export interface HeapLayout {
  nodes: Map<string, NodeLayout>;
  /** Total canvas size needed to fit every node. */
  width: number;
  height: number;
}

// Spacing between columns (depth) and rows (siblings). These are generous so
// boxes of varying size don't collide; the stage scrolls if it overflows.
const COL_GAP = 190; // horizontal distance between depth levels
const ROW_GAP = 130; // vertical distance between stacked nodes
const PAD = 16;

/** The heap-object ids a given object points at, in field/cell order. */
function childIdsOf(obj: HeapObject): string[] {
  const ids: string[] = [];
  if (isArray(obj)) {
    for (const el of obj.elements) {
      if (isRef(el) && el.target && el.target.kind === "heap") {
        ids.push(el.target.id);
      }
    }
  } else if (isStruct(obj)) {
    for (const f of obj.fields) {
      if (isRef(f.value) && f.value.target && f.value.target.kind === "heap") {
        ids.push(f.value.target.id);
      }
    }
  }
  return ids;
}

/** Heap objects referenced directly by a stack variable (the layout roots). */
function rootIds(state: ProgramState): string[] {
  const roots: string[] = [];
  const seen = new Set<string>();
  for (const frame of state.stack) {
    for (const v of frame.variables) {
      if (isRef(v.value) && v.value.target && v.value.target.kind === "heap") {
        const id = v.value.target.id;
        if (!seen.has(id)) {
          seen.add(id);
          roots.push(id);
        }
      }
    }
  }
  return roots;
}

/**
 * Compute positions for every heap object via BFS from the roots. Each node's
 * depth is its shortest distance from a root; nodes are packed into vertical
 * "slots" per depth so siblings don't overlap. Returns absolute positions and
 * the canvas size.
 */
export function layoutHeap(state: ProgramState): HeapLayout {
  const heap = state.heap;
  const allIds = Object.keys(heap);
  const nodes = new Map<string, NodeLayout>();

  // Assign a depth to every node via BFS. CRITICAL ordering: we must fully
  // explore from the real stack roots FIRST (so children get their correct
  // depth), and only THEN seed any still-unvisited objects (unreachable /
  // leaked) as fresh depth-0 roots. Seeding everything up front would wrongly
  // pin every object at depth 0 (a flat column, not a tree).
  const depth = new Map<string, number>();
  const byDepth = new Map<number, string[]>();
  const queue: string[] = [];
  let head = 0;

  const enqueueRoot = (id: string) => {
    if (!depth.has(id) && heap[id]) {
      depth.set(id, 0);
      queue.push(id);
    }
  };

  // Drain the queue with BFS, recording first-reach order per depth.
  const drain = () => {
    while (head < queue.length) {
      const id = queue[head++];
      const d = depth.get(id) ?? 0;
      if (!byDepth.has(d)) byDepth.set(d, []);
      byDepth.get(d)!.push(id);

      const obj = heap[id];
      if (!obj) continue;
      for (const childId of childIdsOf(obj)) {
        if (!depth.has(childId) && heap[childId]) {
          depth.set(childId, d + 1);
          queue.push(childId);
        }
      }
    }
  };

  // 1) Explore from the real roots to completion.
  rootIds(state).forEach(enqueueRoot);
  drain();

  // 2) Any object still unvisited is unreachable from a stack root; seed it as
  //    its own depth-0 root (stable order) and explore its subgraph too.
  for (const id of allIds) {
    if (!depth.has(id)) {
      enqueueRoot(id);
      drain();
    }
  }

  // Place nodes: x by depth, y by order within the depth column. We vertically
  // center each column so the whole diagram reads as balanced.
  const depths = [...byDepth.keys()].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  let maxRows = 0;
  for (const d of depths) maxRows = Math.max(maxRows, byDepth.get(d)!.length);
  const canvasHeight = Math.max(1, maxRows) * ROW_GAP;

  for (const d of depths) {
    const column = byDepth.get(d)!;
    const colHeight = column.length * ROW_GAP;
    const yStart = (canvasHeight - colHeight) / 2;
    column.forEach((id, i) => {
      nodes.set(id, {
        id,
        depth: d,
        x: PAD + d * COL_GAP,
        y: PAD + yStart + i * ROW_GAP,
      });
    });
  }

  const width = PAD * 2 + (depths.length > 0 ? (Math.max(...depths) + 1) * COL_GAP : 0);
  const height = PAD * 2 + canvasHeight;

  return { nodes, width, height };
}

# Error-handling map of the C interpreter backend

Pipeline: `mod.rs::run` (c/mod.rs:107-137) drives `lexer::lex` -> `parser::Parser::parse_program` -> `interp::Interp::new(&program).run()`. Each stage's native error is converted into a single `CError { stage, message, line, kind }` and `main.rs::run_handler` (main.rs:78-108) turns that into the JSON `{ ok:false, errors:[{severity,message,line,stage,kind}] }`.

## 1. LEXER errors (`LexError`, c/lexer.rs)
All carry a real 1-based `line` (the lexer tracks `line`). Messages and triggers:

- `"unexpected character '<c>'"` — c/lexer.rs:303-307. Any byte that is not whitespace, `#`, a comment, an identifier/keyword start, a digit, `'`, `"`, or a recognized operator/punctuation. This is the catch-all `other =>` arm of the single-char operator match. (e.g. `@`, `$`, `|` alone, `~`, `^`, `[` is fine but `\` is not).
- `"unterminated char literal"` — c/lexer.rs:201-204 (EOF right after opening `'`) and c/lexer.rs:217-219 (missing closing `'`).
- `"unterminated escape"` — c/lexer.rs:208-210 (char literal, backslash then EOF) and c/lexer.rs:238-240 (string literal, backslash then EOF).
- `"unterminated string literal"` — c/lexer.rs:250-252 (reached EOF before closing `"`).
- `"invalid float literal '<text>'"` — c/lexer.rs:177-180 (`text.parse::<f64>()` fails; e.g. `1.2.3`).
- `"invalid integer literal '<text>'"` — c/lexer.rs:183-186 (`text.parse::<i64>()` fails; realistically only integer overflow of i64, since the scanner only collects digits).

## 2. PARSER errors (`ParseError`, c/parser.rs)
All carry `self.line()` (the current token's line). The dominant source is `eat()` (c/parser.rs:188-201), which emits the **generic** format `"expected {:?}, found {:?}"` using the Rust `Tok` Debug name — this is why `classify_parse` substring-matches on `Semicolon`, `RParen`, etc.

- `"expected {:?}, found {:?}"` — c/parser.rs:194-197. Raised by every `eat(&Tok::X)` call. The `{:?}` renders the enum variant name (`Semicolon`, `LParen`, `RParen`, `LBrace`, `RBrace`, `LBracket`, `RBracket`, `Colon`, `KwStruct`, `KwTypedef`, etc.). Callers: struct body/`;`/braces (parse_struct_body 110-120, parse_struct_def 124-131, parse_typedef 135-160), function parens/braces (parse_function 283-303), block close (parse_block_body 307-313), `return/break/continue ;` (parse_stmt 335-358), array `]` (parse_var_decl 372-410), `if/while/for` parens (parse_if/while/for 414-480), ternary `:` (parse_ternary 503-517), index `]` (parse_postfix 640), grouping `)` (parse_primary 700), call `)` (parse_primary 735), sizeof `)` (parse_unary 610-625).
- `"expected identifier, found {:?}"` — c/parser.rs:268-271 (`expect_ident`), used for struct/typedef names, field names, function names, param names, and `.`/`->` member names.
- `"expected a type, found {:?}"` — c/parser.rs:256-259 (`parse_type` fell through its match). Triggered when a type is required (function return, params, var-decl via `is_type_start`, struct fields, cast-ish positions) but the token isn't a type keyword / known struct name / `size_t`.
- `"unexpected token in expression: {:?}"` — c/parser.rs:738-741 (`parse_primary` catch-all). Triggered by a stray operator/keyword where a primary expression was expected.

Note: the parser never panics on EOF because `advance()` saturates at the last token (c/parser.rs:177-182) and that last token is always `Eof`; a premature EOF surfaces as an `eat`/`expect_ident` "expected X, found Eof".

## 3. INTERPRETER errors (`RuntimeError`, c/interp.rs)
**Critical fact about lines:** only THREE runtime errors carry a non-zero line; every other one is hard-coded `line: 0`.
- `"no 'main' function found"` — c/interp.rs:201-205, `line: 0`.
- `"call stack overflow (recursion too deep)"` — c/interp.rs:257-261, carries `line` (the call-site line passed into `call_function`). **But** every internal `call_function`/`eval_call` call passes `line: 0` (eval_call at :769-778 calls `self.call_function(func, evaled, 0)`, and `run()` starts main with `0`), so in practice this is also 0.
- `"execution step limit exceeded (possible infinite loop)"` — c/interp.rs:318-322, carries `stmt_line(stmt)` — a **real** line. This is the one runtime error that reliably reports where.

All of the following are `line: 0`:
- `"division by zero"` — c/interp.rs:704 (integer `/` with RHS `as_i64()==0`). Note: float division does NOT check (c/interp.rs:699 `BinOp::Div if use_float`), so `1.0/0.0` yields `inf`, no error.
- `"modulo by zero"` — c/interp.rs:710.
- `"dereferenced a null pointer"` — c/interp.rs:629-633 (`*p` where p is `Pointer(None)`); and `"cannot dereference a non-pointer"` at :633-637 (deref of a scalar/void).
- `"dereferenced a null pointer (->)"` — c/interp.rs:942-946 (`p->field` with null p).
- `"cannot assign through a null pointer"` — c/interp.rs:850-854 (`*p = ...` with null p); `"cannot assign through a null/invalid pointer"` at :854-858 (`*x = ...` where x isn't a pointer).
- `"use of undeclared variable '<n>'"` — c/interp.rs:838-842 (lvalue), :878-882 (index base), :1132-1136 (`read_ident`).
- `"call to unknown function '<n>'"` — c/interp.rs:769-773.
- `"array index N out of bounds (len M)"` — c/interp.rs:912-916.
- `"negative array index"` — c/interp.rs:870-874.
- Shape/aux errors: `"'<n>' is not an array or pointer"` (:886-890), `"indexing a non-array expression"` (:898-902), `"invalid assignment target"` (:860-864), `"not a member access"` (:928-932), `"left of -> is not a struct pointer"` (:948-952), `"left of . is not a struct"` (:965-969, :973-977), `"struct '<T>' has no field '<f>'"` (:985-989), `"member access on a non-struct heap object"` (:991-995), `"variable '<n>' not found"` (:1025-1029), `"dangling heap reference"` (:1034-1038), `"struct field '<f>' not found"` (:1046-1050, :1109-1113), `"field read on a non-struct heap object"` (:1051-1055), `"write to dangling heap reference"` (:1085-1089), `"write to a non-struct heap object"` (:1103-1107).
- `"__exit__"` — c/interp.rs:758: NOT a user error. `run()` (c/interp.rs:208-210) intercepts it and finishes the trace successfully. Any code after `exit()` in the same unwinding path is unreachable, exactly as intended.

## 4. Classification (`mod.rs`) — which kinds exist, and what falls through
`classify_lex` (c/mod.rs:23-35) -> kinds: `lex_unexpected_char`, `lex_unterminated_string`, `lex_unterminated_char` (matches "unterminated char" OR "unterminated escape"), `lex_invalid_number` (matches "invalid integer" OR "invalid float"), else `lex_error`. Lexer coverage is complete — no lexer message falls through to `lex_error`.

`classify_parse` (c/mod.rs:39-66) -> `parse_missing_semicolon`, `parse_missing_rparen`, `parse_missing_lparen`, `parse_missing_rbrace`, `parse_missing_lbrace`, `parse_missing_rbracket`, `parse_expected_identifier`, `parse_expected_type`, `parse_unexpected_in_expr`, else `parse_error`. **Fall-through to generic `parse_error`:** any `eat()` failure whose expected token is not one of the brace/paren/bracket/semicolon set — e.g. `"expected Colon, ..."` (missing `:` in a ternary), `"expected Comma, ..."`, `"expected KwStruct, ..."` (in typedef), `"expected Star/Assign, ..."`. These get only weak coaching. The `expected RBracket`/`LBracket` matches rely on `{:?}` printing exactly `RBracket`/`LBracket`, which it does.

`classify_runtime` (c/mod.rs:71-100) -> `index_out_of_bounds` ("out of bounds"), `negative_index` ("negative array index"), `division_by_zero`, `modulo_by_zero`, `null_deref` ("null pointer" OR "null/invalid pointer"), `undeclared_variable`, `unknown_function` ("unknown function"), `stack_overflow` ("recursion too deep" OR "call stack overflow"), `infinite_loop` ("infinite loop" OR "step limit"), `no_main` ("no 'main'"), else `runtime_other`.
**Ordering gotcha:** the `"out of bounds"` check comes first, so `negative_index` is only reachable because the negative message doesn't contain "out of bounds" — fine. **Fall-through to generic `runtime_other`** (weak coaching) for a large set of real interpreter errors: `"cannot dereference a non-pointer"`, `"'<n>' is not an array or pointer"`, `"indexing a non-array expression"`, `"invalid assignment target"`, `"left of -> is not a struct pointer"`, `"left of . is not a struct"`, `"struct '<T>' has no field '<f>'"`, `"struct field '<f>' not found"`, `"member access on a non-struct heap object"`, `"field read on a non-struct heap object"`, `"variable '<n>' not found"`, `"dangling heap reference"`, `"write to dangling heap reference"`, `"write to a non-struct heap object"`, `"not a member access"`. Notably **"call to unknown function"** matches on substring `"unknown function"` — the message literally reads "call to unknown function '<n>'", which DOES contain "unknown function", so it classifies correctly as `unknown_function`.

## 5. GAPS — things C should flag that this interpreter does NOT

These are verified against code paths, not assumed:

1. **Wrong argument count is silently ignored.** `call_function` (c/interp.rs:263-271) does `func.params.iter().zip(args.into_iter())`. `zip` stops at the shorter side: too few args => trailing params are simply never inserted into the frame (and later reads of them raise the generic `"use of undeclared variable"`/`runtime_other`, not an arity error); too many args => extras are silently dropped. No error is ever produced for arity mismatch.

2. **No type checking at all.** `exec_var_decl` (c/interp.rs:380-470) and `write_location` (c/interp.rs:1061-1130) coerce freely via `coerce_scalar`/`coerce_to_kind`. Assigning a `double` to an `int`, a pointer where a scalar is expected, etc., just coerces (`as_i64`, `& 0xff`). `int *p = 5;` — the `Some(e)` arm at c/interp.rs:432-440 evaluates 5, sees a non-zero scalar, and the `_ => Slot::Pointer(None)` branch silently makes it a NULL pointer. No diagnostic.

3. **Use-before-assignment is not detectable.** A declaration with no initializer gets a default (`default_scalar` 0 / `'\0'`, or `Pointer(None)`) — c/interp.rs:460-466 and :442. So reading an uninitialized local returns 0 instead of flagging undefined behavior. There is no "uninitialized" sentinel in `Slot`.

4. **Missing return / falling off end of non-void.** `call_function` (c/interp.rs:294-300): if `exec_block` returns `Flow::Normal` (no return hit), `ret = RValue::Void`. Falling off the end of `main` or any non-void function is accepted; the caller that uses the result just gets `Void` (treated as 0 by `eval_scalar`/`scalar_from`). Returning a value from a void function is likewise unchecked — `Stmt::Return(Some(e))` is evaluated regardless of `func.ret`. The `ret` type is retained (`Frame.ret_type`) but only used to type `return malloc(...)` (c/interp.rs:383-404), never to validate.

5. **Dereferencing an uninitialized (non-null) pointer.** Only `Pointer(None)` is caught (c/interp.rs:629, :942, :850). But an uninitialized pointer IS `Pointer(None)` here (default), so that case collapses into null_deref — there's no notion of a wild/garbage pointer. A pointer set to a bogus integer can't happen because integer->pointer assignment becomes NULL (gap #2).

6. **Integer overflow is silent.** All integer arithmetic uses plain `+`/`-`/`*` on `i64` (c/interp.rs:701-707). In debug builds Rust would panic (uncaught -> 500-style thread panic, not a `CError`); in release it wraps. Either way there is no `RuntimeError` for overflow.

7. **Reading past end of stdin — does not exist yet.** There is no stdin/`scanf`/`getchar` support anywhere; `eval_call` (c/interp.rs:730-778) special-cases only `printf`, `malloc`, `free`, `exit`, `perror`. So this is greenfield (see section 7).

8. **Redeclaration / shadowing.** `exec_var_decl` always does `frame.slots.insert(...)` and `frame.order.push(...)` (c/interp.rs:450-468). A second declaration of the same name overwrites the slot silently but pushes the name onto `order` again (so it would appear twice in the trace's variable list). No "redeclaration" error. Also note `find_var_frame` (c/interp.rs:1140-1148) only ever looks at the TOP frame and has no block-level scoping, so inner-block declarations leak to the whole function and there's no true shadowing.

9. **Unknown printf format specifier.** `eval_printf` (c/interp.rs:830-838, the `_ =>` arm) does NOT consume an argument and just prints `%` + the spec char literally. So `%z` prints "%z" and the argument alignment for later specifiers silently shifts — no error. Also `%s` always prints the literal `"(str)"` and `%p` prints `"(ptr)"` (strings/pointers aren't really modeled).

10. **Struct field that doesn't exist IS caught** (`"struct '<T>' has no field '<f>'"`, c/interp.rs:985-989) — but classifies as `runtime_other` (gap in classification, section 4), so weak coaching.

11. **`free` is a no-op** (c/interp.rs:754-756): the heap object is kept, so use-after-free and double-free are never detected; a freed pointer keeps working.

12. **Division by zero only for integers** (float `/0` -> `inf`, section 3). Modulo of floats isn't possible (Mod always goes integer path, c/interp.rs:709-713).

## 6. How errors reach the API (and the line-number reality)
`mod.rs::run` maps each stage error into `CError` (c/mod.rs:107-137). Lexer/parser errors always set `line: Some(e.line)`. Runtime errors go through `line: if e.line == 0 { None } else { Some(e.line) }` (c/mod.rs:133-136) — so a `RuntimeError` with `line:0` becomes JSON with **no `line` field** (ApiError's `line: Option<usize>` is `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"`, main.rs:33-35). Per section 3, essentially every runtime error is `line:0` EXCEPT the step-limit/infinite-loop error (`stmt_line(stmt)`), so the frontend AlertPanel will show a line number for infinite loops but NOT for division-by-zero, null-deref, OOB, undeclared-variable, unknown-function, or any field/shape error. `main.rs::run_handler` (main.rs:78-108) wraps the single `CError` into `errors: vec![ApiError{ severity:"error", message, line, stage, kind }]` and returns HTTP 200 with `{ ok:false, errors:[...] }`. (Only one error is ever reported — the pipeline stops at the first failure.) Unknown languages return `kind:"unsupported_language"`, `severity:"info"` (main.rs:100-107).

## 7. Where to hook stdin / scanf / getchar
**Dispatch point:** `eval_call` in c/interp.rs:730-778. The special-case chain is `if name == "printf" {...}` / `"malloc"` / `"free"` / `"exit"` / `"perror"`, then the fallthrough that looks up a user function (`self.functions.get(name)`, c/interp.rs:769-773). Add `"scanf"` / `"getchar"` / `"fgets"` branches here, before the user-function lookup.

**Interp struct fields:** c/interp.rs:159-172 (`program, functions, structs, frames, heap, next_heap_id, states, stdout, step_counter`). There is a `stdout: String` for output but **no input buffer** — add something like `stdin: Vec<char>` + a cursor (or a `String` + index), initialized in `Interp::new` (c/interp.rs:175-199). Reading past the end should produce a new classified `RuntimeError` (e.g. message containing "end of input" and a matching `classify_runtime` arm + kind, since right now it would fall to `runtime_other`).

**Writing through a pointer (what scanf needs):** scanf must write into the location its pointer args point at. The machinery already exists:
- `&x` (address-of) is `UnOp::AddrOf` -> `eval_unary` c/interp.rs:619-622 returns `RValue::Pointer(Some(loc))` where `loc = self.lvalue_of(inner)` (c/interp.rs:835-865). For a local this is `Location::Local{frame,name}`; for `&arr[i]` it resolves to `Location::HeapCell`; for `&s->field` to `Location::HeapField`.
- To store into it, evaluate each scanf arg with `eval_expr` to get an `RValue::Pointer(Some(loc))`, then call `self.write_location(&loc, RValue::Scalar(parsed))` (c/interp.rs:1061-1130). `write_location` already handles `Local`, `HeapCell` (with element coercion), and `HeapField`, so scanf into `&x`, `&arr[i]`, and `&node->field` will all work by reusing it. Guard against the `Pointer(None)` case (null arg) by reusing the existing null-deref error style.

So: add an input buffer field + cursor, branch in `eval_call`, parse from the buffer, and `write_location` through the pointer args — that's the complete hook surface.

RELEVANT FILES (ranked by importance):
  1. backend/src/c/interp.rs — Source of all RuntimeErrors, the eval_call dispatch for stdin hooking, Interp struct fields, and the address-of/write_location machinery scanf needs.
  2. backend/src/c/mod.rs — Defines CError and the classify_lex/parse/runtime kind mapping; shows which messages fall through to generic buckets and how runtime line:0 becomes a missing JSON line.
  3. backend/src/c/lexer.rs — Every LexError message and the exact condition that triggers it.
  4. backend/src/c/parser.rs — Every ParseError message (mostly the generic eat() "expected X, found Y") and the arity-relevant param parsing.
  5. backend/src/main.rs — Shows the final JSON shape {ok,errors:[{severity,message,line,stage,kind}]} and the Option-line serialization that drops line:0.

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct RuntimeError {
    pub message: String,
    pub line: usize,
}

/// A runtime scalar.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
enum Scalar {
    Int(i64),
    Double(f64),
    Char(char),
}

impl Scalar {
    fn as_i64(&self) -> i64 {
        match self {
            Scalar::Int(i) => *i,
            Scalar::Char(c) => *c as i64,
            Scalar::Double(d) => *d as i64,
        }
    }

    fn as_f64(&self) -> f64 {
        match self {
            Scalar::Int(i) => *i as f64,
            Scalar::Char(c) => *c as i64 as f64,
            Scalar::Double(d) => *d,
        }
    }

    fn truthy(&self) -> bool {
        match self {
            Scalar::Int(i) => *i != 0,
            Scalar::Char(c) => *c != '\0',
            Scalar::Double(d) => *d != 0.0,
        }
    }

    fn display(&self) -> String {
        match self {
            Scalar::Int(i) => i.to_string(),
            Scalar::Char(c) => format!("'{}'", c.escape_default()),
            Scalar::Double(d) => format!("{}", d),
        }
    }

    fn type_name(&self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Scalar::Int(_) => "int",
            Scalar::Char(_) => "char",
            Scalar::Double(_) => "double",
        }
    }
}

    pub fn run(mut self) -> Result<ExecutionTrace, RuntimeError> {
        let main = self.functions.get("main").copied().ok_or(RuntimeError {
            message: "no 'main' function found".into(),
            line: 0,
        })?;
        match self.call_function(main, Vec::new(), 0) {
            Ok(_) => Ok(ExecutionTrace { states: self.states }),
            // `exit(code)` unwinds here: finish the trace successfully rather
            // than reporting a runtime error.
            Err(e) if e.message == "__exit__" => Ok(ExecutionTrace { states: self.states }),
            Err(e) => Err(e),
        }
    }

    /// Allocate a default-initialized heap struct of the named type, returning
    /// its heap id. Scalars default to 0; pointers default to null. Unknown
    /// types get an empty struct so the program can still run.
    fn alloc_struct(&mut self, type_name: &str) -> String {
        let id = self.fresh_heap_id("node");
        let mut fields: Vec<(String, Slot)> = Vec::new();
        if let Some(def) = self.structs.get(type_name).copied() {
            for (ty, fname) in &def.fields {
                let slot = if ty.pointer_depth > 0 {
                    Slot::Pointer(None)
                } else {
                    Slot::Scalar(default_scalar(&ty.base))
                };
                fields.push((fname.clone(), slot));
            }
        }
        self.heap.insert(
            id.clone(),
            HeapObjectRuntime::Struct(HeapStruct {
                type_name: type_name.to_string(),
                fields,
            }),
        );
        id
    }

    // ---- heap helpers -----------------------------------------------------

    fn fresh_heap_id(&mut self, prefix: &str) -> String {
        let id = format!("{}_{}", prefix, self.next_heap_id);
        self.next_heap_id += 1;
        id
    }

    // ---- function call ----------------------------------------------------

    fn call_function(
        &mut self,
        func: &'a Function,
        args: Vec<RValue>,
        line: usize,
    ) -> Result<RValue, RuntimeError> {
        if self.frames.len() > 100 {
            return Err(RuntimeError {
                message: "call stack overflow (recursion too deep)".into(),
                line,
            });
        }

        let mut frame = Frame {
            function_name: func.name.clone(),
            order: Vec::new(),
            slots: HashMap::new(),
            declared: HashMap::new(),
            ret_type: func.ret.clone(),
        };

        for (param, arg) in func.params.iter().zip(args.into_iter()) {
            let slot = match arg {
                RValue::Scalar(s) => Slot::Scalar(coerce_scalar(s, &param.ty.base)),
                RValue::Pointer(p) => Slot::Pointer(p),
                RValue::Void => Slot::Scalar(Scalar::Int(0)),
            };
            frame.order.push(param.name.clone());
            frame.slots.insert(param.name.clone(), slot);
            frame.declared.insert(param.name.clone(), param.ty.clone());
        }

        self.frames.push(frame);

        // Entry snapshot: anchor a state at this function's own call depth
        // before its first statement runs. This guarantees every depth level
        // has a state at its entry point, which the frontend debugger relies
        // on for intuitive step-into / step-over / step-out behavior (otherwise
        // a function whose first action is itself a call would have no state at
        // its own depth until after the nested call returned).
        let entry_line = func.body.first().map(stmt_line).filter(|l| *l != 0);
        self.snapshot(entry_line, Some(format!("Enter {}()", func.name)));

        let flow = self.exec_block(&func.body)?;
        let ret = match flow {
            Flow::Return(v) => v,
            _ => RValue::Void,
        };

        self.frames.pop();
        Ok(ret)
    }

    // ---- statements -------------------------------------------------------

    fn exec_block(&mut self, stmts: &[Stmt]) -> Result<Flow, RuntimeError> {
        for stmt in stmts {
            let flow = self.exec_stmt(stmt)?;
            if !matches!(flow, Flow::Normal) {
                return Ok(flow);
            }
        }
        Ok(Flow::Normal)
    }

    fn exec_stmt(&mut self, stmt: &Stmt) -> Result<Flow, RuntimeError> {
        self.step_counter += 1;
        if self.step_counter > MAX_STEPS {
            return Err(RuntimeError {
                message: "execution step limit exceeded (possible infinite loop)".into(),
                line: stmt_line(stmt),
            });
        }

        match stmt {
            Stmt::VarDecl {
                ty,
                name,
                array_len,
                init,
                array_init,
                line,
            } => {
                self.exec_var_decl(ty, name, *array_len, init, array_init, *line)?;
                self.snapshot(Some(*line), Some(format!("Declared {}", name)));
                Ok(Flow::Normal)
            }
            Stmt::ExprStmt(expr, line) => {
                self.eval_expr(expr)?;
                self.snapshot(Some(*line), None);
                Ok(Flow::Normal)
            }
            Stmt::If {
                cond,
                then_branch,
                else_branch,
                line,
            } => {
                let c = self.eval_scalar(cond)?;
                self.snapshot(Some(*line), Some(format!("if (...) -> {}", c.truthy())));
                if c.truthy() {
                    self.exec_block(then_branch)
                } else if let Some(eb) = else_branch {
                    self.exec_block(eb)
                } else {
                    Ok(Flow::Normal)
                }

                let loc = self.lvalue_of(inner)?;
                Ok(RValue::Pointer(Some(loc)))
            }
            UnOp::Deref => {
                let v = self.eval_expr(inner)?;
                match v {
                    RValue::Pointer(Some(loc)) => self.read_location(&loc),
                    RValue::Pointer(None) => Err(RuntimeError {
                        message: "dereferenced a null pointer".into(),
                        line: 0,
                    }),
                    _ => Err(RuntimeError {
                        message: "cannot dereference a non-pointer".into(),
                        line: 0,
                    }),
                }
            }
        }
    }

    fn eval_binary(&mut self, op: &BinOp, l: &Expr, r: &Expr) -> Result<RValue, RuntimeError> {
        // Short-circuit logicals.
        if let BinOp::And = op {
            let lv = self.eval_scalar(l)?;
            if !lv.truthy() {
                return Ok(RValue::Scalar(Scalar::Int(0)));
            }
            let rv = self.eval_scalar(r)?;
            return Ok(RValue::Scalar(Scalar::Int(if rv.truthy() { 1 } else { 0 })));
        }
        if let BinOp::Or = op {
            let lv = self.eval_scalar(l)?;
            if lv.truthy() {
                return Ok(RValue::Scalar(Scalar::Int(1)));
            }
            let rv = self.eval_scalar(r)?;
            return Ok(RValue::Scalar(Scalar::Int(if rv.truthy() { 1 } else { 0 })));
        }

        // Equality/inequality may involve pointers (e.g. `root == NULL`).
        if matches!(op, BinOp::Eq | BinOp::Ne) {
            let lr = self.eval_expr(l)?;
            let rr = self.eval_expr(r)?;
            if matches!(lr, RValue::Pointer(_)) || matches!(rr, RValue::Pointer(_)) {
                let eq = pointers_equal(&lr, &rr);
                let res = match op {
                    BinOp::Eq => eq,
                    _ => !eq,
                };
                return Ok(RValue::Scalar(Scalar::Int(bool_i(res))));
            }
            // Neither is a pointer: fall through to scalar comparison using the
            // already-evaluated values.
            let lv = scalar_from(lr);
            let rv = scalar_from(rr);
            let use_float = matches!(lv, Scalar::Double(_)) || matches!(rv, Scalar::Double(_));
            let eq = if use_float {
                lv.as_f64() == rv.as_f64()
            } else {
                lv.as_i64() == rv.as_i64()
            };
            let res = match op {
                BinOp::Eq => eq,
                _ => !eq,
            };
            return Ok(RValue::Scalar(Scalar::Int(bool_i(res))));
